newsitem.title: RUSSIA: LUKoil ups product exports, leading Russian rivals.
newsitem.headline: LUKoil ups product exports, leading Russian rivals.

text.p: LUKoil, Russia's largest oil company, is working flat out to boost oil product output and exports this year, but rival Russian majors are lagging in the drive towards value-added products, oil analysts said on Monday.
LUKoil spokesman Pyotr Neyev said rising global demand for oil products and favourable economics for exporting oil products as opposed to crude were behind the firm's policy.

"Yes, there is a policy at LUKoil to export more products than crude, because it is advantageous to the company," he said. "Oil products are more profitable to sell than crude oil, and demand for products on the world market is growing."
Neyev's comments followed LUKoil first-quarter results showing a massive 53 percent leap in oil product exports from year-ago levels to 1.4 million tonnes.
The figure is roughly in line with LUKoil's stated aim of exporting 6.0 million tonnes of products in 1997, up 33 percent from 4.5 million tonnes delivered in 1996.
LUKoil's refineries processed 4.8 million tonnes (384,000 bpd) of oil in the first three months of the year, with another 1.0 million tonnes (80,000 bpd) coming from tolling operations.
LUKoil plans to boost refinery throughput this year by three percent to 19.8 million tonnes (396,000 bpd).
Analysts said other Russian oil companies were also looking to boost refinery runs in 1997 but said LUKoil was keeping well ahead of its Russian rivals.

"The LUKoil management has hit the mark in terms of recognising the importance of products," said Dan Lubash, managing director of Emerging Markets Europe at Merrill Lynch in London. "LUKoil, as usual, is a couple of steps ahead of the pack."
If LUKoil's planned downstream investments came off, the company could double refinery throughput to around 800,000 barrels per day in the medium term, he said.
Lubash said Russian oil product output and exports would rise in 1997 but that the rate of increase would not match LUKoil's first-quarter performance.

The rate of increase in total Russian oil product exports during the first quarter of 1997 lagged behind LUKoil's but still weighed with an impressive 43 percent jump year-on-year to 13 million tonnes, State Statistics Committee figures show.
LUKoil's Neyev said the company was aiming to improve the quality as well as the quantity of its oil products.
"LUKoil is looking to improve the quality of its oil products to bring them into line with European standards," he said. "We've already made major investments in this direction."
Late last year LUKoil said it spent $250 million on a vacuum distillation unit capable of processing 1.6 million tonnes of heavy fuel oil a year at the Permnefteorgsintez refinery.
LUKoil also plans to invest in improving product quality at the Norsi refinery, in which it is seeking a bigger stake, Neyev said.
Analysts said that boosting products output made sense both in terms of exports and supplying the domestic market.
Lubash said Russia's product pipeline system was less full than burgeoning crude oil routes, allowing product exports to rise. And in the long term demand would start to recover.
"There is a big amount of pent-up demand, and an extremely good chance for companies to earn real cash from product exports until the Russian market recovers," he said.
Neyev said Russian demand showed no sign of picking up during the first quarter of the year, adding that LUKoil's crude output would be closely linked to domestic demand in 1997.
"If our oil is not used to fill rising demand on the internal market, then we will depend heavily on how much we can export, and as you know export possibilities are limited."

A harsh tax regime for oil producers could also dent oil output in 1997, he said. Russian oil production has nearly halved since peaking in the late 1980s, slumping to 293 million tonnes (5.86 million bpd) last year.
